Belavadös Time Conversion Guide
Earth-first table play, Belavadös-second lore time
1. The New Rule
Use Earth dates and Earth time first for players, schedules, sessions, travel, and deadlines.
Use Belavadös dates second for lore, temples, festivals, legal records, journals, and immersion.
A Belavadös year is 330.15 Belavadös solar days long. For table play, those 330.15 days are distributed evenly across the Earth year.
2. Clean Math

365 days, or 366 days in leap years

blocks.text: 3. Conversion Formula
daysInEarthYear = 365, or 366 in a leap year.
earthProgress = (Earth day-of-year - 1 + fractionOfEarthDay) / daysInEarthYear.
belSolarDayProgress = earthProgress x 330.15. Use this for sky, moon, season, and astronomy math.
belCivilDateProgress = earthProgress x 330. Use this for the named calendar date.
monthIndex = floor(belCivilDateProgress / 30), from 0 to 10.
dayOfMonth = floor(belCivilDateProgress % 30) + 1.
Belavadös clock time may use the fractional part of belSolarDayProgress x 24.

rows: Important distinction: the Night Sky uses the astronomical year of 330.15 Belavadös days. The civil calendar still has 330 named dates. The extra 0.15 is distributed through the year as a tiny solar/clock correction, not stored as a bonus day at the end.

6. Night Sky Integration
Use 330.15 Belavadös days as the astronomical year because the Night Sky file identifies Belavadös at 1.00 AU with a 330.15-day orbital period.
Use 330 named civil dates for the calendar because the civil calendar is still 11 months of 30 days.
Use solar progress, not month/date progress, for moon phases, planetary positions, constellations, tides, and sky omens.

The larger moon Chandratecu-Seleneš has a 19.20 Belavadös-day orbit; the smaller moonlet Mictlindra-Nannara has a 2.02 Belavadös-day orbit. For Earth sessions, calculate their phase from belSolarDayProgress so the sky stays smooth all year.
Because the solar correction is distributed, the Star-River, wandering worlds, and paired moons never need a special frozen/end-buffer period.

1. Guide and sky-time rules
Naming and replacement rules used in this document
• The bright band crossing the sky is called the Star-River of Belavadös.
• The observing landscape is described as the Great River Valley and its desert-edge skyfields.
• The twelve wandering planets and two moons use the supplied invented names and coordinates.

Coordinate system used

The sky is described with right ascension and declination. These coordinates function like celestial longitude and latitude. Apparent magnitude uses lower numbers for brighter objects, with negative values being especially bright. Planet and moon distances use AU or kilometers; stellar distances use light-years.

blocks.text: 2. Sky setting and Star-River
Historical-style sky setting
The analysis assumes a view from approximately 30° N latitude. At 30° N, stars above about +60° declination are circumpolar, while stars below about -60° declination never rise.

The sky looks dark, dense, and sharply structured. With no electric skyglow, the Star-River of Belavadös would have been a major visible feature rather than a faint haze. Bright planets, bright stars, both moons, and future named sky patterns can serve as seasonal markers, navigation guides, calendar anchors, and story-bearing landmarks.
The Star-River of Belavadös

The Star-River of Belavadös is the luminous band of unresolved stars and dark rifts crossing the night sky. In summer evenings, it would stretch through the southern gate-and-serpent sectors and climb toward the northern seasonal markers. In winter evenings, it would run near the Bronze Bull region, becoming paler but still visible under dry, dark conditions.

From desert-edge skyfields, the Star-River would not have appeared as a smooth strip. It would have looked mottled, braided, and broken by dark channels. The brightest warm-season section would have been low-to-mid in the southern sky; the higher northern section would have served as a nightly path for visual navigation.

The names are the names carved into tide stairs, burial ledgers, cairn roads, hearth beams, watchtower lintels, reef shrines, and desert-edge observatories.
Each figure keeps its fixed place in the sky. The names belong to Belavadös. The coordinates preserve the star-path for sky maps, generators, omen records, and night watches.
4.1. How skykeepers read the fixed heavens

Belavadös skykeepers use right ascension and declination as the fixed grid of the upper world. Right ascension runs from 0h to 24h around the sky. Declination rises north or south of the sky-equator. Magnitude records visible brightness; the smaller the number, the stronger the light.

Seasonal movement follows the 330.15 day Belavadös solar year. Civil dates still belong to the eleven named months, but the sky obeys solar progress. Moon phases, tides, wandering worlds, Star-River omens, and constellation seasons move smoothly across the whole year.

The old horizon rule is simple enough for any watchtower: at about 30 degrees north, lights above about +60 degrees stay near the northern sky and lights below about -60 degrees never rise. Other latitudes shift the height of the figures without moving the figures themselves.

rows: Age of Open Gods: The oldest names are devotional, practical, and fearful. They belong to farmers reading harvest weather, sailors reading tide and reef, caravan guides reading desert night, burial clerks reading Nefarokir's ledger, and temple astronomers watching for the moods of hungry divine powers.

blocks.text: 4.5. Skykeeper practice

Harbors, caravan wells, funeral roads, terrace farms, reef shrines, and high watchtowers all keep different portions of the same sky. Coastal settlements read Bastveig's Tidehook, Freyseth's Mask, the Star-River, and the two moons for water law. The old rule remains unchanged: a constellation is a witness. A vow spoken beneath a named figure is never only private. The sky is a ledger, a road, a tide stair, a battlefield, a mirror, a hearth, and a warning. When the Gods were free, this was not metaphor. It was daily survival.
5. Two moons in the Belavadös sky

The lunar system is nested: the larger moon orbits the world, while the smaller moonlet orbits the larger moon and is carried along with it. Mictlindra-Nannara is now one-third of its former linear size and follows a steep retrograde orbit around Chandratecu-Seleneš. This creates paired lunar calendars, tiny bead-like crossings, and a very small secondary tide-timing pulse rather than a major second tide. For Earth sessions, both lunar positions are calculated from belSolarDayProgress, not from the civil month and date.

Moonlet revision for program update: Mictlindra-Nannara is now one-third its former diameter (544 km instead of 1,633 km), with matching one-third circumference and approximately one-twenty-seventh former volume/mass. Its orbit around Chandratecu-Seleneš is retrograde and steeply angled, using inclination i = 125° relative to the primary moon's prograde orbital plane. In code, this means reverse the moonlet angular direction and rotate the moonlet orbit ring, not the world or the constellation sphere.

Mictlindra-Nannara phase = (belSolarDayProgress mod 2.02) / 2.02.

blocks.text: 8. Representative night

A representative high-era observing night can be generated by first calculating belSolarDayProgress from the Earth date and local observing time, then placing Chandratecu-Seleneš and Mictlindra-Nannara along their 19.20-day and 2.02-day cycles. A sample scene may place the paired lunar system near RA 06h 15m and Dec +18° to +19°, close to the northern cold-season field and high enough for easy viewing from 30° N. Mictlindra-Nannara should appear as a tiny copper bead moving backward along a steeply tilted path around the primary moon.

When the bright inner planet Mardukesh-Huitra is favorably placed, it dominates the evening or dawn sky with pearl-white brilliance. Surixoch-Aresu appears copper-red and lower near twilight. The four ringed planets are not equally easy to interpret with the unaided eye, but under magnification their ring lore becomes central: Vishtecu-Hyperu shows a rose-gold hairline, Enlimitra a frosted silver span, Quetzal-Hermeshu a tilted green-bronze eye, and Varunatl-Kronu a white-ringed blue elongation.

10. Research Update: Constellation Distances and Globe-in-Constellation Integration

Purpose of this update. This section adds the distance logic needed to place the Belavados globe program inside the constellation program without breaking astronomical scale, RA/Dec sky behavior, moon behavior, or the existing Belavados sky lore.

Core correction. A constellation does not live at one distance from Earth or Belavados. It is an Earth-viewed angular pattern or sky region. Its stars and nebulae sit at many different true distances along the same sightlines. For programming, that means the constellation layer must be rendered as an angular sky shell around the world/camera while storing real distance metadata for zooms, lore, brightness, parallax, and future deep-space transitions.

1. Narrative Summary: The Safe Giant That Still Looks Terrifying

Eiršu'neth is not a timid little fleck of ice. It is a giant cometary body: a porous, icy, volatile-rich nucleus approximately 137 km across, large enough to be treated as a named celestial actor rather than an anonymous periodic visitor. In sky-lore terms, it is the kind of comet that gets its own festivals, sailors' superstitions, observatory careers, and political arguments about omen interpretation.

Mathematically, the expanded version now has two modes that must not be confused. The legacy compact path was a moderate outer-family ellipse, while the active constellation-layer path keeps the 2.08 AU perihelion and extends the outer turn to Nephthysra's Mirror at 54,000 ly. That makes the true-scale ellipse extremely eccentric, with e = 0.999999998782, and requires a logarithmic or segmented render mode for any playable globe/constellation simulation.

The most important safety fact is not simply that the comet is outside Vishtecu-Hyperu at perihelion. It is that the only points where the comet crosses the main Celestial Road plane are the two orbital extremes: perihelion and aphelion. Everywhere between, the body is above or below the plane, so even when its radial distance overlaps the broad planetary neighborhoods of the middle outer system, it is vertically displaced from those traffic lanes.

This document therefore treats Eiršu'neth as a safe giant comet with deliberately exaggerated analytical care. Every major attribute is paired with the equation that generates it, the unit conversion that makes it readable, and the simulation parameter that can be used in an HTML or game-engine implementation.

blocks.text: 5. Keplerian Position Math
M = E - e*sin(E)
E_next = E - (E - e*sin(E) - M)/(1 - e*cos(E))
nu = 2*atan2(sqrt(1+e)*sin(E/2), sqrt(1-e)*cos(E/2))
x_orb = a(cos(E) - e)
y_orb = b*sin(E)

In the coordinate form above, the Sun is already at one focus. That is convenient for rendering because the comet position is heliocentric without needing to draw an ellipse centered on the star incorrectly.
6. 3D Inclination and Celestial Road Crossings

The orbital plane is tilted by 18°. The simplest clean implementation rotates the orbital-plane y-coordinate into vertical height z. The longitude of the ascending node can then be used as an artistic spin angle to keep the visible orbit from overlapping other stylized paths.
x = x_orb*cos(Omega) - y_orb*cos(i)*sin(Omega)
y = x_orb*sin(Omega) + y_orb*cos(i)*cos(Omega)
z = y_orb*sin(i)
z = r*sin(nu)*sin(i)
z_max near r ~ a: z_max ~= a*sin(i) = 3.475*sin(18°) = 1.074 AU

The crossings happen when z = 0. With this orientation, z = 0 when sin(nu) = 0, which occurs at nu = 0° and nu = 180°: perihelion and aphelion. This is the clean mathematical reason the comet can radially pass through the outer system without behaving like a collision threat.

blocks.text: 8. Speed, Vis-Viva, and Why the Comet Dramatically Accelerates

Eiršu'neth's speed is governed by the vis-viva equation. It is not simply 'fast' or 'slow': it is fastest at perihelion, slowest at aphelion, and continuously trades potential energy for kinetic energy along the arc.
v = sqrt(mu*(2/r - 1/a))
v(r) = v_1AU*sqrt(2/r - 1/a), where v_1AU = 32.95 km/s
v_p = 27.05 km/s at r = 2.08 AU
v_a = 11.55 km/s at r = 4.87 AU

9. Orbital Energy and Angular Momentum
specific orbital energy: epsilon = -mu/(2a)
specific angular momentum: h = sqrt(mu*a*(1 - e^2))
perihelion angular momentum check: h = r_p*v_p
aphelion angular momentum check: h = r_a*v_a

Those last two checks explain the inverse relationship between distance and tangential speed at the endpoints: at the closer endpoint r is smaller, so v must be larger to preserve angular momentum. At the farther endpoint r is larger, so v is smaller.

blocks.text: 14. Radiation Pressure and Beta

The key parameter for dust-tail formation is beta: the ratio of solar radiation pressure acceleration to solar gravitational acceleration. A high-beta grain behaves as though the Sun's gravity is strongly reduced; a low-beta grain behaves more like a tiny inertial pebble following the comet's path.
beta = F_rad/F_grav
mu_dust = mu_star*(1 - beta)
a_rad = beta*mu_star/r^2
beta ~= C_pr*Q_pr/(rho_d*s)
r_dust(t) is solved as a Kepler problem with mu replaced by mu*(1 - beta)

The important simulation consequence is that different grain sizes do not share the comet's orbit after release. The dust fan is a memory of emission times and grain sizes, not a static triangle glued behind the comet.
15. Syndynes and Synchrones

A syndyne is the locus of grains with the same beta value emitted at different times. A synchrone is the locus of grains emitted at the same time with different beta values. Together, these curves are the mathematical skeleton behind a dust tail's curved, layered appearance.

For a detailed HTML or offline renderer, Eiršu'neth can use a Monte Carlo particle tail. Each simulated particle receives a release time, size, beta, ejection velocity, emission direction, albedo weight, and lifetime. blocks.text: 17. Brightness and Photometry Model

A visually convincing comet must be bright for mathematical reasons, not just because the renderer paints it bright. The simplest useful brightness weight combines grain cross section, albedo, phase behavior, heliocentric distance, observer distance, and opacity falloff.
cross section per grain: G = pi*s^2
particle brightness weight: B_i proportional to p_v(alpha)*Phi(alpha)*G/(r_h^2*Delta^2)
surface brightness pixel: I(x,y) = sum_i B_i * PSF(x-x_i,y-y_i)
optical depth proxy: tau = sum_i G_i / pixel_area
extinction through tail: I_star,out = I_star,in*exp(-tau)

25. Lore Integration Without Breaking the Math

Eiršu'neth can be terrifying to ordinary people while still being safe to astronomers. This is useful worldbuilding: a comet can be emotionally dangerous, politically dangerous, religiously dangerous, and navigationally significant without being physically on an impact trajectory.
A 6.48-year return is short enough for people to remember multiple apparitions within a lifetime, but long enough to make each passage feel ceremonial.
The perihelion near Vishtecu-Hyperu invites ring-watching festivals because the comet brightens just outside that family's region.
The 18° inclination gives the visual impression of a blade cutting across the Celestial Road rather than a tame object sliding along the same flat track as everything else.
The nucleus is so large that cultures could argue whether it is a comet, a wandering frost-world, an omen-beast, or a divine remnant.
Mathematically literate sky-watchers can reassure the public: the danger is spectacle, not collision.

Appendix F. Radiation Pressure, Beta, and Grain-Size Obsession

The dust tail is not a decorative cone. It is a sorting machine. Solar radiation pressure sorts grains by beta, beta is mostly a function of size and density, and the visible tail is the integrated history of that sorting process.
beta = F_rad/F_grav
a_dust = -mu_star*(1 - beta)*r_vec/|r|^3
beta_small_grain > beta_large_grain
for beta = 0: dust follows normal solar gravity
for 0 < beta < 1: dust is still attracted to the Sun, but weakly
for beta = 1: radiation pressure cancels solar gravity in the radial idealization
for beta > 1: effective central force becomes repulsive and fine grains are blown outward rapidly
approx beta(s) = C/(rho_d*s), so doubling grain radius halves beta if density is fixed

Appendix G. Dust Emission Probability Distributions
A serious tail simulation needs probability distributions. The comet's tail is made of many draws from these distributions, not one hand-placed ribbon.
size distribution: dN/ds = K*s^(-alpha), s_min <= s <= s_max
inverse-CDF sample if alpha != 1: s = [u*(s_max^(1-alpha)-s_min^(1-alpha)) + s_min^(1-alpha)]^(1/(1-alpha))
mass distribution per size bin: dM/ds proportional to s^3*dN/ds = K*s^(3-alpha)
cross-section distribution per size bin: dA/ds proportional to s^2*dN/ds = K*s^(2-alpha)
activity weighting: W(t) = W0*(q/r(t))^m * seasonalJet(t) * outburst(t)
jet angular distribution: P(theta) proportional to exp[-theta^2/(2*sigma_jet^2)]
isotropic background venting: direction = random point on sphere
sunward hemisphere venting: accept direction d only if dot(d, sunward_normal) > 0

Appendix H. Outbursts, Shells, Jets, and Tail Memory
Because Eiršu'neth is huge, it can support localized vents and episodic outbursts. These create shells and bands in the tail. A painterly tail becomes more realistic if it is not smooth everywhere.
outburst(t) = 1 + A_burst*exp[-(t - t_burst)^2/(2*sigma_t^2)]
shell radius after emission: R_shell ~= v_emit*(t_obs - t_emit)
projected shell thickness: sigma_shell ~= sigma_v*(t_obs - t_emit)
band brightness: B_band proportional to M_burst/(4*pi*R_shell^2)
jet precession phase: phi_jet(t) = phi0 + omega_spin*t + omega_precession*t
active longitude modulation: W_lon = max(0, dot(surface_normal, sun_direction))^eta
dust memory time: t_memory grows as beta decreases
High-beta grains are the comet's recent mood: they show what the Sun is doing to the finest material right now.
Low-beta grains are the comet's memory: they record older emissions near the orbital path.
Outburst shells can be used as in-world omens because they create visible bands, knots, or feathered layers.
A single nucleus can produce multiple tails if jets emit grains with different beta distributions or if viewing geometry separates the dust sheets.

flux ratio to magnitude: m2 - m1 = -2.5*log10(F2/F1)

m_comet = H + 5*log10(Delta) + 2.5*n_h*log10(r_h) + phase_term(alpha)
surface brightness per pixel: mu = ZP - 2.5*log10(F_pixel/pixel_area_arcsec2)
coma profile proxy: I(rho) = I0/(rho + rho0)^k
tail fade proxy: I(s) = I0*exp(-s/L_tail)/(1 + s/s0)^k

Appendix J. Formal Safety Proof in Plain Language and Symbols
This proof is intentionally over-formal for worldbuilding, because the whole point is to make the safety of a terrifying comet mathematically satisfying.
Let the Celestial Road be the z=0 plane.
Let the comet orbit be inclined with z = r*sin(nu)*sin(i), where i = 18°.
Plane crossing requires z = 0.
Since i != 0, z = 0 requires sin(nu) = 0.
Therefore nu = 0° or 180° only.
At nu = 0°, r = q = 2.08 AU, which is outside Vishtecu-Hyperu's 1.88 AU orbit by 0.20 AU.
At nu = 180°, r = Q = 4.87 AU, which remains inside Quetzal-Hermeshu's 5.31 AU region by 0.44 AU.
At all other nu, z != 0, so radial overlap does not imply same-plane intersection.
Conclusion: Eiršu'neth is visually dramatic but non-impacting under the intended two-body inclined-orbit model.

blocks.text: Appendix M. How to Tell If the Comet Has Been Rendered Wrong
If the comet crosses the Celestial Road at any point other than perihelion or aphelion, the inclination transform is wrong.
If the comet moves at constant visible angular speed, the engine is using true anomaly incorrectly instead of solving Kepler's equation.
If the tail points along the velocity vector only, the ion tail is wrong; the first-order direction should be anti-solar.
If the dust tail is perfectly straight, the dust model is too simple; dust should curve because particles remember previous comet positions and have beta-dependent paths.
If the nucleus is true-scale in a solar-system view, it will be invisible; labels should use physical scale, visuals should use clamped/exaggerated scale.
If the comet threatens Vishtecu-Hyperu, q or the planet orbit was changed incorrectly; the canonical radial clearance is 0.20 AU.
If the comet reaches Quetzal-Hermeshu's orbit, Q was changed incorrectly; the canonical outer margin is 0.44 AU inside 5.31 AU.
If old dust vanishes immediately, the particle lifetime is too short; low-beta grains should form a persistent orbital trail.
If all particles have the same transparency, the tail lacks mass sorting; brightness should depend on cross section, beta, age, r_h, Delta, and phase angle.
